claims.text: The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr RHEA is a single-phase BCC alloy with high density and low room-temperature ductility.
The baseline alloy has a density of approximately 12-13 g/cm3.
The baseline alloy has a yield strength of approximately 1000 MPa.
The baseline alloy has less than 5% room-temperature ductility.
Adding 0.5-2.0 at% Si or Al can induce a secondary intermetallic phase in Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr.
The induced phase is likely to be B2-type Hf-Ti-Al when Al is added or Laves-type Hf-Ti-Si when Si is added.
Heat treatment at approximately 1000-1200°C for 24 hours will promote formation of a reticulated intermetallic network at grain boundaries and within the BCC matrix.
BCC solid solutions can decompose during high-temperature processing to form Laves phases, including precipitates at grain boundaries.
A secondary B2 phase dispersed in a continuous BCC matrix can improve room-temperature compressive ductility while maintaining high yield strength.
A continuous ordered B2 matrix in two-phase RHEAs is associated with poor room-temperature ductility.
A reticulated intermetallic network will deflect and branch cracks along tortuous phase boundaries, increasing fracture area and energy absorption.
Solid-solution hardening primarily raises yield strength and often reduces ductility in BCC RHEAs.
The secondary phase will increase compressive yield strength by 10-20%.
The reticulated network will increase room-temperature plastic strain to failure from less than 5% to more than 10-15%.
Modified-alloy density will remain within 1-2% of the baseline; Al may reduce it slightly, whereas Si will leave it similar.
The proposed operating regime is uniaxial compression at room temperature, approximately 25°C.
Ductility enhancement requires a continuous or semi-continuous reticulated network; isolated particles or coarse brittle films may instead promote intergranular fracture and reduce ductility.
Comparing a network-containing Si alloy with a quenched, nominally single-phase Si alloy can distinguish network-mediated toughening from solid-solution hardening.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis initially describes the trade-off as a slight density increase, but elsewhere predicts neutral-to-lower density, particularly for Al, and density remaining within 1-2% of baseline.

The proposed benefit is assigned to a continuous or semi-continuous intermetallic network, while the cited B2 evidence attributes poor ductility to a continuous ordered B2 matrix and improved ductility to discrete B2 precipitates. The hypothesis does not reconcile these opposing morphology implications.
